Where it began

Sandeep Patil was born in Bombay on 18 August 1956 and grew up in the Shivaji Park area of the city. Sport ran in the family. His father, Madhusudan Patil, played first-class cricket and badminton at national level, and was good at tennis and football too. His coach was Ankush 'Anna' Vaidya.

As a young man he was as much a bowler as a batsman, sending down medium pace off the wrong foot. He joined the Bombay Ranji side in 1975–76, and his first big innings came in the 1979 semi-final against Delhi: 145, with the side in trouble.

The player

Runs for West Zone against the touring Australians and Pakistanis earned him a Test call in 1979–80. A week before his debut he hit 210 from 205 balls against Saurashtra at the Wankhede, and his last six sailed out of the ground altogether.

Patil played 29 Tests for India from 1980 to 1984, scoring 1,588 runs at 36.93 with four hundreds and seven fifties. The best of them was 174 at Adelaide, at that time the highest innings by an Indian in Australia. He was man of the match on his one-day international debut, with 64 against Australia. Best of all, he was part of the side that won the 1983 World Cup, making 216 runs in the tournament, among them an unbeaten 51 in the semi-final against England. India won the Asia Cup the following year with him in the team.

What made him special

Patil loved to hit the ball hard. The innings people remember came in a Test at Manchester. With India close to following on, he took six fours from a single over by Bob Willis, one of them off a no-ball, racing from 73 to 104 in nine balls. Rain ended the game with him on 129 not out.

His bowling was more of a sideline. He took nine Test wickets in all, though he did once share the new ball with Kapil Dev, at Auckland. Not every part-time medium pacer can say that.

Away from the middle

After leaving Tests he led Madhya Pradesh from 1988 to 1993. He went on to coach India and India A, and in 2003 he guided Kenya, very much outsiders, all the way to a World Cup semi-final. He later ran the National Cricket Academy, and from 2012 to 2016 he chaired India's selection committee.

He kept busy off the field too. He wrote an autobiography, Sandy Storm, in 1984, and edited the Marathi sports magazine Ekach Shatkar, which for a time was a best-seller in Maharashtra. The popular newspaper Mahanagar began life in his garage.

And finally

Soon after the 1983 triumph, Patil was offered the leading role in a Bollywood film, Kabhie Ajnabi The, which came out in 1985. His World Cup team-mate Syed Kirmani played the villain, and the film made much of a fight scene between the two. Cricket proved to be his stronger suit, but very few World Cup winners can say they traded punches with a team-mate on the big screen.
